## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. For any fixed $p \ge 1$, we can choose $q$ (specifically, any $q > 2p+1$ for which $\sum n^q a_n$ converges) so that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^p \sqrt{a_n}$ converges.

**Setup.** Since $\sum n^q a_n$ converges for arbitrarily large $q$, the set of such $q$ is unbounded above. Fix $p \ge 1$ and pick $q > 2p+1$ with $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^q a_n < \infty$.

**Key step (Cauchy–Schwarz).** Write
$$n^p \sqrt{a_n} = \bigl(n^{q/2}\sqrt{a_n}\bigr)\cdot n^{\,p - q/2},$$
so by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^p \sqrt{a_n} \;\le\; \Bigl(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^q a_n\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{2p-q}\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$

**First factor.** $\sum n^q a_n < \infty$ by our choice of $q$.

**Second factor.** Since $q > 2p+1$, we have $2p - q < -1$, i.e. $q - 2p > 1$. Thus
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{2p-q} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^{q-2p}}$$
is a convergent $p$-series (exponent $q - 2p > 1$).

**Conclusion.** Both factors on the right-hand side are finite, hence
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^p \sqrt{a_n} < \infty.$$

Therefore, choosing any $q > 2p+1$ for which $\sum n^q a_n$ converges guarantees the convergence of $\sum n^p \sqrt{a_n}$. $\blacksquare$
